newsitem.title: CHINA: HK protesters vow more marches, demand elections.
newsitem.headline: HK protesters vow more marches, demand elections.

text.p: Pro-democracy activists vowed to stage more protests in Hong Kong on Tuesday and called on communist China to hold immediate legislative elections.
"In the eyes of the world, we call on the Chinese government to allow free, fair and democratic elections immediately," said pro-democracy leader Martin Lee.
He was speaking to thousands of supporters at the building of the old elected legislature, dissolved by Beijing when Hong Kong was handed over by Britain at midnight on Monday.
Democracy activists poured into the streets during the handover ceremonies, staging boisterous rallies and vowing to fight for civil liberties.

"The message is that we want democracy and we want it now," said leader Emily Lau at a rally in Statue Square. She led hundreds of people around the legislature, wrapping the building with a giant yellow ribbon.
"The yellow ribbon is our wish that democracy returns," said Lee Cheuk-yan, another prominent campaigner.
A number of groups had vowed to stage the first protests on Tuesday to test the limits of political freedoms now that Hong Kong was again part of communist China.
Lee, leader of the popular Democratic Party, issued his challenge for elections from the balcony of the legislative building.
He spoke shortly before a new 60-member Beijing-appointed assembly was sworn in at a ceremony shunned by U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and British Prime Minister Tony Blair.
"We pledge to continue to be the voice of Hong Kong People -- in or out of office -- and to fight to get democracy back," Lee said.
The Beijing-approved legislature, meeting for the first time on Hong Kong soil, quickly passed an omnibus bill activating laws it had adopted ahead of the formal handover to China.
The bill approved a string of laws, including controversial curbs on political protests and the funding of political parties.
Lee and other activists said these measures would hurt their chances in legislative elections which Hong Kong's new leader, Tung Chee-hwa, has said will be held next May.
Pro-democracy groups have strongly criticised the curbs on political reforms introduced near the end of British rule.
Rita Fan, the chamber's president, told legislators that in the next few months they should try to pass an electoral law so that elections could be held as soon as possible.
